the President's visit, fitting it with a heliport, which he smashed with a sledgehammer after the rejection. Despite the
snub, when Sinatra learned of Kennedy's assassination, he reportedly sobbed in his bedroom for three days. Sinatra
worked with Hubert H. Humphrey in 1968, and remained a supporter of the Democratic Party until the early 1970s.
Although still a registered Democrat, Sinatra endorsed <color=#3366CC>Republican</color> Ronald Reagan for a second term as governor of
California in 1970. Sinatra officially changed allegiance in July 1972 when he supported <color=#3366CC>Richard Nixon</color> in the 1972
presidential election.
In the 1980 presidential election, Sinatra donated $4 million to Ronald Reagan's campaign. Sinatra arranged Reagan's
Presidential gala, as he had done for Kennedy. In 1985, Reagan presented Sinatra with the Presidential Medal of
Freedom, remarking, "His love of country, his generosity for those less fortunate ... make him one of our most
remarkable and distinguished Americans."
On June 18, 1984, Sinatra performed at the state dinner in the White House honoring Sri Lankan president <color=#3366CC>J. R.</color>
<color=#3366CC>Jayewardene</color> at the invitation of Reagan, singing "Strangers in the Night" and "Fly Me to the Moon".
Santopietro notes that Sinatra was a "lifelong sympathizer with Jewish causes." He was awarded the Hollzer Memorial
Award by the Los Angeles Jewish Community in 1949. Sinatra gave a series of concerts in Israel in 1962 and donated
his entire $50,000 fee for appearing in a cameo role in Cast a Giant Shadow (1966) to the Youth Center in Jerusalem.
On November 1, 1972, Sinatra raised $6.5 million in bond pledges for Israel, and was given the Medallion of Valor. The
Frank Sinatra Student Center at the <color=#3366CC>Hebrew University of Jerusalem</color> was dedicated in 1978.
From his youth, Sinatra displayed sympathy for black Americans and worked both publicly and privately all his life to
help the struggle for equal rights. He blamed racial prejudice on the parents of children. Sinatra played a major role in
the <color=#3366CC>desegregation</color> of <color=#3366CC>Nevada</color> hotels and casinos in the 1950s and 1960s. On January 27, 1961, Sinatra played a
benefit show at Carnegie Hall for <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther King Jr.</color> and led his fellow Rat Pack members and Reprise label mates
in boycotting hotels and casinos that refused entry to black patrons and performers. According to his son, Frank Jr.,
King sat weeping in the audience at one of his father's concerts in 1963 as Sinatra sang "<color=#3366CC>Ol' Man River</color>", a song from
the musical <color=#3366CC>Show Boat</color> that is sung by a black American stevedore.
Death and funeral
During the final years of his life, Sinatra was in ill health and was frequently hospitalized for <color=#3366CC>heart</color> and <color=#3366CC>breathing</color>

<color=#3366CC>problems</color>, <color=#3366CC>high blood pressure</color>, <color=#3366CC>pneumonia</color>, and bladder cancer. He made no public appearances following a <color=#3366CC>heart</color>
<color=#3366CC>attack</color> in February 1997. On the evening of May 14, 1998, Sinatra died in his sleep at age 82 after suffering another
heart attack at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles, with his wife Barbara at his side. Barbara encouraged
Sinatra to "fight" while attempts were made to stabilize him, and reported that Sinatra's final words were, "I'm losing."
His daughter, Tina, later wrote that she and her siblings had not been notified of their father's final hospitalization, and it
was her belief that "the omission was deliberate. Barbara would be the grieving widow alone at her husband's side."
The night after Sinatra's death, the lights on the <color=#3366CC>Empire State Building</color> were turned blue, the lights at the <color=#3366CC>Las Vegas</color>
<color=#3366CC>Strip</color> were dimmed, and the casinos stopped spinning for one minute. Significant increases in recording sales
worldwide were reported by Billboard in the month of Sinatra's death.
Sinatra's funeral was held at the Church of the Good Shepherd in Beverly Hills, California, on May 20, 1998, with 400
mourners in attendance and thousands of fans outside. <color=#3366CC>Gregory Peck</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tony Bennett</color>, and Sinatra's son, Frank Jr.,
addressed the mourners.
Sinatra was buried in a blue business suit and a red and blue necktie because of his support for the Italian football club
Genoa CFC; his grave, adorned with mementos from family members, was next to his parents in Desert Memorial Park
in Cathedral City, California. The phrases "The Best Is Yet to Come", and "Beloved Husband & Father" were placed on
Sinatra's modest grave marker. Sinatra's gravestone was changed as of 2021 to read "Sleep Warm, Poppa", due to
damage to the original gravestone.
Legacy and honors
<color=#3366CC>Robert Christgau</color> referred to Sinatra as "the greatest singer of the 20th century". His popularity is surpassed only by
<color=#3366CC>Elvis Presley</color>, <color=#3366CC>the Beatles</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Michael Jackson</color>. For Santopietro, Sinatra was the "greatest male pop singer in the
history of America", who amassed "unprecedented power onscreen and off", and "seemed to exemplify the common
man, an ethnic twentieth-century American male who reached the 'top of the heap', yet never forgot his roots."
Santopietro argues that his career was centered around power, perfecting the ability to capture an audience. He
continues to be regarded as an iconic figure.
Gus Levene commented that Sinatra's strength was that when it came to lyrics, telling a story musically, Sinatra
displayed a "genius" ability and feeling, which with the "rare combination of voice and showmanship" made him the
"original singer" which others who followed most tried to emulate. George Roberts, a trombonist in Sinatra's band,
remarked that Sinatra had a "charisma, or whatever it is about him, that no one else had." Biographer Arnold Shaw
considered that "If Las Vegas had not existed, Sinatra could have invented it." He quoted reporter James Bacon in
saying that Sinatra was the "swinging image on which the town is built", adding that no other entertainer quite
"embodied the glamour" associated with Las Vegas. Sinatra is seen as one of the icons of the 20th century, and has
three stars on the <color=#3366CC>Hollywood Walk of Fame</color>.
In Sinatra's native Hoboken, he was awarded the Key to the City on October 30, 1947. In 2003, the city's main post
office was rededicated in his honor. A bronze plaque, placed two years before Sinatra's death, marks the site of the
house where he was born. There is also a marker in front of Hoboken Historical Museum, which has artifacts from his
life and conducts Sinatra walking tours. Frank Sinatra Drive runs parallel to the Hudson River Waterfront Walkway. On
the waterfront is Frank Sinatra Park, where a bronze plaque was placed in 1989 upon its opening. In the Frank Sinatra
Park, a 6 ft tall bronze statue of Sinatra was dedicated in 2021 on December 12, Sinatra's birthday. A residence hall at
Montclair State University in New Jersey was named in his honor. Other buildings named for Sinatra include the Frank
Sinatra School of the Arts in Astoria, Queens, the Frank Sinatra International Student Center at <color=#3366CC>Hebrew University</color> in
Jerusalem, and the Frank Sinatra Hall at the USC School of Cinematic Arts in Los Angeles. Wynn Resorts' Encore Las
Vegas resort features a restaurant dedicated to Sinatra which opened in 2008. There are several roadways named in
honor of Frank Sinatra in several states of the U.S.
Memorabilia from Sinatra's life and career, including awards, gold records, and personal items, are displayed at USC’s
Frank Sinatra Hall in Los Angeles and at the Sinatra restaurant at Encore at Wynn Las Vegas.
The United States Postal Service issued a stamp in honor of Sinatra in May 2008, commemorating the tenth
anniversary of his death. In May 2008, the <color=#3366CC>United States Congress</color> designated May 13 as Frank Sinatra Day.
Sinatra received three honorary degrees during his lifetime. In May 1976, he was invited to speak at the University of
Nevada, Las Vegas graduation commencement and was bestowed an Honorary Doctorate litterarum humanarum.
During his speech, Sinatra stated that his education had come from "the school of hard knocks" and that "this is the first
educational degree I have ever held in my hand. I will never forget what you have done for me today". In 1984 and
1985, Sinatra received an Honorary Doctorate of Fine Arts from Loyola Marymount University and an Honorary
Doctorate of Engineering from the Stevens Institute of Technology.
In 2023, <color=#3366CC>Rolling Stone</color> ranked Sinatra at No. 19 on their list of the 200 Greatest Singers of All Time.
In 2024, a new road in North <color=#3366CC>Bristol</color> was named Sinatra Way, to commemorate Sinatra's 1953 visit to Frenchay
Hospital.

Film, television and stage portrayals
A television miniseries based on Sinatra's life, titled Sinatra, was aired by CBS in 1992. The series was directed by
James Steven Sadwith, who won an Emmy Award for Outstanding Individual Achievement in Directing for a Miniseries
or a Special and starred Philip Casnoff as Sinatra. Sinatra was written by Abby Mann and Philip Mastrosimone and
produced by Sinatra's daughter, Tina.
Sinatra has subsequently been portrayed on screen by Ray Liotta (The Rat Pack, 1998), James Russo (Stealing
Sinatra, 2003), <color=#3366CC>Dennis Hopper</color> (The Night We Called It a Day, 2003), and Robert Knepper (My Way, 2012), and
spoofed by Joe Piscopo and <color=#3366CC>Phil Hartman</color> on <color=#3366CC>Saturday Night Live</color>. A biographical film directed by <color=#3366CC>Martin Scorsese</color> has
long been planned. Alex Gibney directed a four-part biographical series on Sinatra, All or Nothing at All, for HBO in
2015. A musical tribute was aired on <color=#3366CC>CBS</color> television in December 2015 to mark Sinatra's centenary. Sinatra was also
portrayed by Rico Simonini in the 2018 feature film Frank & Ava, which is based on a play by Willard Manus. Creed
singer Scott Stapp also portrayed Sinatra in the 2024 feature film Reagan, a biopic of U.S. President <color=#3366CC>Ronald Reagan</color>.
Martin Scorsese planned to make a film on Sinatra and his second wife Ava Gardner.
In 2021, Sinatra was portrayed by actor Frank John Hughes in the Paramount+ limited series, The Offer.
Sinatra believed that Johnny Fontane, a mob-associated singer in <color=#3366CC>Mario Puzo</color>'s novel The Godfather (1969), was
based on him. Puzo wrote in 1972 that when the author and singer met in Chasen's, Sinatra "started to shout abuse",
threatening violence. <color=#3366CC>Francis Ford Coppola</color>, director of the <color=#3366CC>film adaptation</color>, said in the audio commentary that
"Obviously Johnny Fontane was inspired by a kind of Frank Sinatra character".
In 2023, Sinatra: The Musical by Joe DiPietro premiered at the Birmingham Repertory Theatre starring Matt Doyle as
Sinatra.

Europe
Europe is a <color=#3366CC>continent</color> located entirely in the <color=#3366CC>Northern Hemisphere</color> and mostly in the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Hemisphere</color>. It is bordered

by the <color=#3366CC>Arctic Ocean</color> to the north, the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color> to the west, the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color> to the south, and <color=#3366CC>Asia</color> to the
east. Europe shares the landmass of <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> with Asia, and of <color=#3366CC>Afro-Eurasia</color> with both <color=#3366CC>Africa</color> and Asia. Europe is
commonly considered to be separated from Asia by the watershed of the <color=#3366CC>Ural Mountains</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Ural River</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Caspian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sea</color>, the Greater Caucasus, the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>, and the Turkish straits.
Europe covers approximately 10,186,000 km2, or 2% of <color=#3366CC>Earth's surface</color> (6.8% of Earth's land area), making it the
second-smallest continent (using the <color=#3366CC>seven-continent model</color>). Politically, Europe is divided into about fifty sovereign
states, of which <color=#3366CC>Russia</color> is the largest and most populous, spanning 39% of the continent and comprising 15% of its
population. Europe had a total population of about million (about 10% of the <color=#3366CC>world population</color>) in; the third-largest after
Asia and Africa. The European climate is affected by warm Atlantic currents, such as the <color=#3366CC>Gulf Stream</color>, which produce a
<color=#3366CC>temperate climate</color>, tempering winters and summers, on much of the continent. Further from the sea, seasonal
differences are more noticeable producing more <color=#3366CC>continental climates</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>culture of Europe</color> consists of a range of national and regional cultures, which form the central roots of the wider
<color=#3366CC>Western civilisation</color>, and together commonly reference <color=#3366CC>ancient Greece</color> and <color=#3366CC>ancient Rome</color>, particularly through their
Christian successors, as crucial and shared roots. Beginning with the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> in 476 CE,
Christian consolidation of Europe in the wake of the <color=#3366CC>Migration Period</color> marked the European <color=#3366CC>post-classical</color> <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Italian Renaissance</color> spread across many <color=#3366CC>Western European</color> countries, adapting to local contexts and giving rise to
distinct national expressions. The renewed humanist emphasis on <color=#3366CC>art</color> and science was among the several factors that
contributed to the broader transition to the modern era. Since the <color=#3366CC>Age of Discovery</color>, led by <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> and <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>, Europe
played a predominant role in global affairs with multiple explorations and conquests around the world. Between the
16th and 20th centuries, European powers colonised at various times the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>, almost all of Africa and <color=#3366CC>Oceania</color>,
and the majority of Asia.
The <color=#3366CC>Age of Enlightenment</color>, the <color=#3366CC>French Revolution</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic Wars</color> shaped the continent culturally, politically,
and economically from the end of the 17th century until the first half of the 19th century. The <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color>,
which began in <color=#3366CC>Great Britain</color> at the end of the 18th century, gave rise to radical economic, cultural, and social change in
<color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color> and eventually the wider world. Both <color=#3366CC>world wars</color> began and were fought to a great extent in Europe,
contributing to a decline in Western European dominance in world affairs by the mid-20th century as the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>
and the United States took prominence and competed over <color=#3366CC>geopolitical dominance</color> in Europe and globally. The

resulting <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color> divided Europe along the <color=#3366CC>Iron Curtain</color>, with <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> in the West and the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> in the <color=#3366CC>East</color>.
This divide ended with the <color=#3366CC>Revolutions of 1989</color>, the <color=#3366CC>fall of the Berlin Wall</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>dissolution of the Soviet Union</color>, which
allowed <color=#3366CC>European integration</color> to advance significantly.
European integration has been advanced institutionally since 1948 with the founding of the <color=#3366CC>Council of Europe</color>, and
significantly through the realisation of the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> (EU), which represents today the majority of Europe. The
European Union is a supranational political entity that lies between a <color=#3366CC>confederation</color> and a <color=#3366CC>federation</color> and is based on a
system of European treaties. The EU originated in Western Europe but has been expanding eastward since the
dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. A majority of its members have adopted a common currency, the <color=#3366CC>euro</color>, and
participate in the <color=#3366CC>European single market</color> and a customs union. A large bloc of countries, the <color=#3366CC>Schengen Area</color>, have
also abolished internal border and immigration controls. Regular popular elections take place every five years within the
EU; they are considered the second-largest democratic elections in the world after India's. The <color=#3366CC>EU economy</color> is the
second-largest in the world by nominal <color=#3366CC>GDP</color> and third-largest by <color=#3366CC>PPP-adjusted GDP</color>.
Etymology
In classical <color=#3366CC>Greek mythology</color>, <color=#3366CC>Europa</color> (Europē) was a <color=#3366CC>Phoenician</color> princess. One view is that her name derives from the
Ancient Greek elements (eurús) 'wide, broad', and (ōps, gen., ōpós) 'eye, face, countenance', hence their composite
Europē would mean 'wide-gazing' or 'broad of aspect'. Broad has been an epithet of Earth herself in the reconstructed
<color=#3366CC>Proto-Indo-European religion</color> and the poetry devoted to it. An alternative view is that of Robert Beekes, who has argued
in favour of a pre-Indo-European origin for the name, explaining that a derivation from eurus would yield a different
toponym than Europa. Beekes has located toponyms related to that of Europa in the territory of ancient Greece, and
localities such as that of Europos in <color=#3366CC>ancient Macedonia</color>.
There have been attempts to connect Europē to a Semitic term for west, this being either <color=#3366CC>Akkadian</color> erebu meaning 'to
go down, set' (said of the sun) or Phoenician 'ereb 'evening, west', which is at the origin of <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> maghreb and <color=#3366CC>Hebrew</color>
ma'arav. <color=#3366CC>Martin Litchfield West</color> stated that "phonologically, the match between Europa's name and any form of the
Semitic word is very poor", while Beekes considers a connection to Semitic languages improbable.
Most major world languages use words derived from Europē or Europa to refer to the continent. Chinese, for example,
uses the word Ōuzhōu, which is an abbreviation of the transliterated name Ōuluóbā zhōu (zhōu means "continent"); a
similar Chinese-derived term Ōshū is also sometimes used in Japanese such as in the Japanese name of the
European Union, Ōshū Rengō, despite the <color=#3366CC>katakana</color> Yōroppa being more commonly used. In some Turkic languages,
the originally Persian name Frangistan ("land of the <color=#3366CC>Franks</color>") is used casually in referring to much of Europe, besides
official names such as Avrupa or Evropa.
Definition
Contemporary definition
Clickable map of Europe, showing one of the most commonly used continental boundaries Key: blue: states which
straddle the border between Europe and Asia; green: countries not geographically in Europe, but closely associated
with the continent
The prevalent definition of Europe as a geographical term has been in use since the mid-19th century. Europe is taken
to be bounded by large bodies of water to the north, west and south; Europe's limits to the east and north-east are

usually taken to be the <color=#3366CC>Ural Mountains</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Ural River</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Caspian Sea</color>; to the south-east, the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color>
<color=#3366CC>Mountains</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>, and the waterways connecting the Black Sea to the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>.
Islands are generally grouped with the nearest continental landmass, hence <color=#3366CC>Iceland</color> is considered to be part of Europe,
while the nearby island of Greenland is usually assigned to <color=#3366CC>North America</color>, although politically belonging to Denmark.
Nevertheless, there are some exceptions based on sociopolitical and cultural differences. Cyprus is closest to <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color>
(or Asia Minor), but is considered part of Europe politically and it is a member state of the EU. Malta was considered an
island of <color=#3366CC>North-western Africa</color> for centuries, but now it is considered to be part of Europe as well. "Europe", as used
specifically in <color=#3366CC>British English</color>, may also refer to <color=#3366CC>Continental Europe</color> exclusively.
The term "continent" usually implies the <color=#3366CC>physical geography</color> of a large land mass completely or almost completely
surrounded by water at its borders. Prior to the adoption of the current convention that includes mountain divides, the
border between Europe and Asia had been redefined several times since its first conception in <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>, but
always as a series of rivers, seas and straits that were believed to extend an unknown distance east and north from the
Mediterranean Sea without the inclusion of any mountain ranges. Cartographer Herman Moll suggested in 1715 that
Europe was bounded by a series of partly joined waterways directed towards the Turkish straits, and the <color=#3366CC>Irtysh River</color>
draining into the upper part of the <color=#3366CC>Ob River</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Arctic Ocean</color>. In contrast, the present eastern boundary of Europe
partially adheres to the Ural and Caucasus Mountains, which is somewhat arbitrary and inconsistent compared to any
clear-cut definition of the term "continent".
The current division of Eurasia into two continents now reflects East-West cultural, linguistic and ethnic differences
which vary on a spectrum rather than with a sharp dividing line. The geographic border between Europe and Asia does
not follow any state boundaries and now only follows a few bodies of water. Turkey is generally considered a
transcontinental country divided entirely by water, while Russia and <color=#3366CC>Kazakhstan</color> are only partly divided by waterways.
France, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain are also transcontinental (or more properly, intercontinental, when oceans
or large seas are involved) in that their main land areas are in Europe while pockets of their territories are located on
other <color=#3366CC>continents</color> separated from Europe by large bodies of water. Spain, for example, has territories (<color=#3366CC>Ceuta</color> and <color=#3366CC>Melilla</color>)
south of the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color> which are parts of <color=#3366CC>Africa</color> and share a border with Morocco. According to the current
convention, Georgia and Azerbaijan are transcontinental countries where waterways have been completely replaced by
mountains as the divide between continents.
History of the concept
Early history
The first recorded usage of Europē as a geographic term is in the Homeric Hymn to <color=#3366CC>Delian Apollo</color>, in reference to the
western shore of the <color=#3366CC>Aegean Sea</color>. As a name for a part of the known world, it is first used in the 6th century BCE by
<color=#3366CC>Anaximander</color> and Hecataeus. Anaximander placed the boundary between Asia and Europe along the Phasis River (the
modern Rioni River on the territory of <color=#3366CC>Georgia</color>) in the Caucasus, a convention still followed by <color=#3366CC>Herodotus</color> in the 5th
century BCE. Herodotus mentioned that the world had been divided by unknown persons into three parts—Europe,
Asia, and Libya (Africa)—with the <color=#3366CC>Nile</color> and the Phasis forming their boundaries—though he also states that some
considered the <color=#3366CC>River Don</color>, rather than the Phasis, as the boundary between Europe and Asia. Europe's eastern frontier
was defined in the 1st century by geographer <color=#3366CC>Strabo</color> at the River Don. The Book of Jubilees described the continents
as the lands given by <color=#3366CC>Noah</color> to his three sons; Europe was defined as stretching from the Pillars of Hercules at the <color=#3366CC>Strait</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Gibraltar</color>, separating it from <color=#3366CC>Northwest Africa</color>, to the Don, separating it from Asia.
The convention received by the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color> and surviving into modern usage is that of the <color=#3366CC>Roman era</color> used by
Roman-era authors such as <color=#3366CC>Posidonius</color>, <color=#3366CC>Strabo</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Ptolemy</color>, who took the Tanais (the modern Don River) as the
boundary.
The Roman Empire did not attach a strong identity to the concept of continental divisions. However, following the fall of
the <color=#3366CC>Western Roman Empire</color>, the <color=#3366CC>culture that developed in its place</color>, linked to Latin and the Catholic church, began to
associate itself with the concept of "Europe". The term "Europe" is first used for a cultural sphere in the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> of the 9th century. From that time, the term designated the sphere of influence of the Western Church, as
opposed to both the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox</color> churches and to the <color=#3366CC>Islamic world</color>.
A cultural definition of Europe as the lands of <color=#3366CC>Latin Christendom</color> coalesced in the 8th century, signifying the new
cultural condominium created through the confluence of Germanic traditions and Christian-Latin culture, defined partly
in contrast with <color=#3366CC>Byzantium</color> and <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>, and limited to northern <color=#3366CC>Iberia</color>, the British Isles, France, Christianised western
Germany, the Alpine regions and northern and central Italy. The concept is one of the lasting legacies of the
<color=#3366CC>Carolingian Renaissance</color>: Europa often figures in the letters of Charlemagne's court scholar, <color=#3366CC>Alcuin</color>. The transition of
Europe to being a cultural term as well as a geographic one led to the borders of Europe being affected by cultural
considerations in the East, especially relating to areas under Byzantine, Ottoman, and Russian influence. Such
questions were affected by the positive connotations associated with the term Europe by its users. Such cultural
considerations were not applied to the Americas, despite their conquest and settlement by European states. Instead,
the concept of "Western civilisation" emerged as a way of grouping together Europe and these colonies.
Modern definitions
The question of defining a precise eastern boundary of Europe arises in the Early Modern period, as the eastern
extension of <color=#3366CC>Muscovy</color> began to include <color=#3366CC>North Asia</color>. Throughout the Middle Ages and into the 18th century, the
traditional division of the landmass of <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> into two continents, Europe and Asia, followed Ptolemy, with the
boundary following the Turkish Straits, the <color=#3366CC>Black Sea</color>, the Kerch Strait, the <color=#3366CC>Sea of Azov</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Don</color> (ancient Tanais).
But maps produced during the 16th to 18th centuries tended to differ in how to continue the boundary beyond the Don
bend at Kalach-na-Donu (where it is closest to the Volga, now joined with it by the <color=#3366CC>Volga–Don Canal</color>), into territory not
described in any detail by the ancient geographers.
Around 1715, Herman Moll produced a map showing the northern part of the <color=#3366CC>Ob River</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Irtysh River</color>, a major
tributary of the Ob, as components of a series of partly joined waterways taking the boundary between Europe and Asia
from the Turkish Straits, and the Don River all the way to the Arctic Ocean. In 1721, he produced a more up to date
map that was easier to read. However, his proposal to adhere to major rivers as the line of demarcation was never
taken up by other geographers who were beginning to move away from the idea of water boundaries as the only
legitimate divides between Europe and Asia.
Four years later, in 1725, Philip Johan von Strahlenberg was the first to depart from the classical Don boundary. He
drew a new line along the <color=#3366CC>Volga</color>, following the Volga north until the Samara Bend, along Obshchy Syrt (the drainage
divide between the Volga and <color=#3366CC>Ural Rivers</color>), then north and east along the latter waterway to its source in the <color=#3366CC>Ural</color>
<color=#3366CC>Mountains</color>. At this point he proposed that mountain ranges could be included as boundaries between continents as
alternatives to nearby waterways. Accordingly, he drew the new boundary north along the Ural Mountains rather than
the nearby and parallel running Ob and Irtysh rivers. This was endorsed by the Russian Empire and introduced the
convention that would eventually become commonly accepted. However, this did not come without criticism. <color=#3366CC>Voltaire</color>,
writing in 1760 about <color=#3366CC>Peter the Great</color>'s efforts to make Russia more European, ignored the whole boundary question
with his claim that neither Russia, Scandinavia, northern Germany, nor Poland were fully part of Europe. Since then,
many modern analytical geographers like <color=#3366CC>Halford Mackinder</color> have declared that they see little validity in the Ural
Mountains as a boundary between continents.
The mapmakers continued to differ on the boundary between the lower Don and Samara well into the 19th century. The
1745 atlas published by the <color=#3366CC>Russian Academy of Sciences</color> has the boundary follow the Don beyond Kalach as far as
Serafimovich before cutting north towards <color=#3366CC>Arkhangelsk</color>, while other 18th- to 19th-century mapmakers such as John
Cary followed Strahlenberg's prescription. To the south, the Kuma–Manych Depression was identified c. 1773 by a
German naturalist, <color=#3366CC>Peter Simon Pallas</color>, as a valley that once connected the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea, and
subsequently was proposed as a natural boundary between continents.
By the mid-19th century, there were three main conventions, one following the Don, the <color=#3366CC>Volga–Don Canal</color> and the
Volga, the other following the Kuma–Manych Depression to the Caspian and then the Ural River, and the third
abandoning the Don altogether, following the Greater Caucasus watershed to the Caspian. The question was still
treated as a "controversy" in geographical literature of the 1860s, with Douglas Freshfield advocating the Caucasus
crest boundary as the "best possible", citing support from various "modern geographers".
In Russia and the <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>, the boundary along the Kuma–Manych Depression was the most commonly used as
early as 1906. In 1958, the Soviet Geographical Society formally recommended that the boundary between the Europe
and Asia be drawn in textbooks from Baydaratskaya Bay, on the <color=#3366CC>Kara Sea</color>, along the eastern foot of Ural Mountains,
then following the <color=#3366CC>Ural River</color> until the Mugodzhar Hills, and then the <color=#3366CC>Emba River</color>; and Kuma–Manych Depression, thus
placing the Caucasus entirely in Asia and the Urals entirely in Europe. The Flora Europaea adopted a boundary along
the Terek and Kuban rivers, so southwards from the Kuma and the Manych, but still with the Caucasus entirely in Asia.
However, most geographers in the Soviet Union favoured the boundary along the Caucasus crest, and this became the
common convention in the later 20th century, although the Kuma–Manych boundary remained in use in some
20th-century maps.
Martin W. Lewis and Kären Wigen argue that the separation of <color=#3366CC>Eurasia</color> into Asia and Europe of vastly uneven sizes
produces a false impression of parity between European and Asian countries, as a residue of <color=#3366CC>Eurocentrism</color>: "In
physical, cultural and historical diversity, China and India are comparable to the entire European landmass, not to a
single European country."
History
Prehistory
During the 2.5 million years of the <color=#3366CC>Pleistocene</color>, numerous cold phases called glacials (<color=#3366CC>Quaternary ice age</color>), or
significant advances of continental ice sheets, in Europe and North America, occurred at intervals of approximately
40,000 to 100,000 years. The long glacial periods were separated by more temperate and shorter interglacials which
lasted about 10,000–15,000 years. The last cold episode of the <color=#3366CC>last glacial period</color> ended about 10,000 years ago. Earth
is currently in an interglacial period of the Quaternary, called the <color=#3366CC>Holocene</color>.
<color=#3366CC>Homo erectus georgicus</color>, which lived roughly 1.8 million years ago in <color=#3366CC>Georgia</color>, is the earliest <color=#3366CC>hominin</color> to have been
discovered in Europe. <color=#3366CC>Other</color> hominin remains, dating back roughly 1 million years, have been discovered in Atapuerca,
<color=#3366CC>Spain</color>. <color=#3366CC>Neanderthal man</color> (named after the Neandertal valley in <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>) appeared in Europe 150,000 years ago
(115,000 years ago it is found already in the territory of present-day <color=#3366CC>Poland</color>) and disappeared from the fossil record
about 40,000 years ago, with their final refuge being the Iberian Peninsula. The Neanderthals were supplanted by
modern humans (<color=#3366CC>Cro-Magnons</color>), who seem to have appeared in Europe around 43,000 to 40,000 years ago. However,
there is also evidence that Homo sapiens arrived in Europe around 54,000 years ago, some 10,000 years earlier than
previously thought. The earliest sites in Europe dated 48,000 years ago are Riparo Mochi (Italy), Geissenklösterle
(Germany) and Isturitz (France).
The <color=#3366CC>European Neolithic</color> period—marked by the cultivation of crops and the raising of livestock, increased numbers of
settlements and the widespread use of pottery—began around 7000 BCE in <color=#3366CC>Greece</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>, probably
influenced by earlier farming practices in <color=#3366CC>Anatolia</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Near East</color>. It spread from the Balkans along the valleys of
the <color=#3366CC>Danube</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Rhine</color> (Linear Pottery culture), and along the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean coast</color> (Cardial culture). Between 4500
and 3000 BCE, these central European neolithic cultures developed further to the west and the north, transmitting
newly acquired skills in producing copper artifacts. In Western Europe the Neolithic period was characterised not by
large agricultural settlements but by field monuments, such as causewayed enclosures, <color=#3366CC>burial mounds</color> and <color=#3366CC>megalithic</color>
<color=#3366CC>tombs</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Corded Ware</color> cultural horizon flourished at the transition from the Neolithic to the <color=#3366CC>Chalcolithic</color>. During this
period giant <color=#3366CC>megalithic</color> monuments, such as the Megalithic Temples of Malta and <color=#3366CC>Stonehenge</color>, were constructed
throughout Western and Southern Europe.
The modern native populations of Europe largely descend from three distinct lineages: Mesolithic <color=#3366CC>hunter-gatherers</color>,
descended from populations associated with the Paleolithic Epigravettian culture; Neolithic Early European Farmers
who migrated from Anatolia during the <color=#3366CC>Neolithic Revolution</color> 9,000 years ago; and <color=#3366CC>Yamnaya</color> Steppe herders who
expanded into Europe from the Pontic–Caspian steppe of Ukraine and southern Russia in the context of <color=#3366CC>Indo-European</color>
<color=#3366CC>migrations</color> 5,000 years ago. The European Bronze Age began c. 3200 BCE in Greece with the <color=#3366CC>Minoan civilisation</color> on
<color=#3366CC>Crete</color>, the first advanced civilisation in Europe. The Minoans were followed by the <color=#3366CC>Myceneans</color>, who collapsed suddenly
around 1200 BCE, ushering the European Iron Age. Iron Age colonisation by the Greeks and <color=#3366CC>Phoenicians</color> gave rise to
early Mediterranean cities. Early Iron Age Italy and <color=#3366CC>Greece</color> from around the 8th century BCE gradually gave rise to
historical Classical antiquity, whose beginning is sometimes dated to 776 BCE, the year of the first <color=#3366CC>Olympic Games</color>.
Classical antiquity
Ancient Greece was the founding culture of Western civilisation. Western <color=#3366CC>democratic</color> and <color=#3366CC>rationalist culture</color> are often
attributed to Ancient Greece. The Greek city-state, the polis, was the fundamental political unit of classical Greece. In
508 BCE, <color=#3366CC>Cleisthenes</color> instituted the world's first <color=#3366CC>democratic</color> system of government in <color=#3366CC>Athens</color>. The Greek political ideals
were rediscovered in the late 18th century by European philosophers and idealists. Greece also generated many

cultural contributions: in <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>humanism</color> and <color=#3366CC>rationalism</color> under <color=#3366CC>Aristotle</color>, <color=#3366CC>Socrates</color> and <color=#3366CC>Plato</color>; in <color=#3366CC>history</color> with
<color=#3366CC>Herodotus</color> and <color=#3366CC>Thucydides</color>; in dramatic and narrative verse, starting with the epic poems of <color=#3366CC>Homer</color>; in drama with

<color=#3366CC>Sophocles</color> and <color=#3366CC>Euripides</color>; in medicine with <color=#3366CC>Hippocrates</color> and <color=#3366CC>Galen</color>; and in science with <color=#3366CC>Pythagoras</color>, <color=#3366CC>Euclid</color>, and
<color=#3366CC>Archimedes</color>. In the course of the 5th century BCE, several of the Greek <color=#3366CC>city states</color> would ultimately check the
<color=#3366CC>Achaemenid Persian</color> advance in Europe through the <color=#3366CC>Greco-Persian Wars</color>, considered a pivotal moment in world
history, as the 50 years of peace that followed are known as Golden Age of Athens, the seminal period of ancient
Greece that laid many of the foundations of Western civilisation.

Greece was followed by <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>, which left its mark on <color=#3366CC>law</color>, <color=#3366CC>politics</color>, <color=#3366CC>language</color>, engineering, <color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, government,
and many more key aspects in western civilisation. By 200 BCE, Rome had conquered Italy and over the following two

centuries it conquered <color=#3366CC>Greece</color>, Hispania (<color=#3366CC>Spain</color> and <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color>), the <color=#3366CC>North African</color> coast, much of the <color=#3366CC>Middle East</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gaul</color>
(<color=#3366CC>France</color> and <color=#3366CC>Belgium</color>), and <color=#3366CC>Britannia</color> (England and <color=#3366CC>Wales</color>).
Expanding from their base in central Italy beginning in the third century BCE, the Romans gradually expanded to
eventually rule the entire Mediterranean basin and Western Europe by the turn of the millennium. The <color=#3366CC>Roman Republic</color>
ended in 27 BCE, when <color=#3366CC>Augustus</color> proclaimed the <color=#3366CC>Roman Empire</color>. The two centuries that followed are known as the
<color=#3366CC>pax romana</color>, a period of unprecedented peace, prosperity and political stability in most of Europe. The empire
continued to expand under emperors such as <color=#3366CC>Antoninus Pius</color> and <color=#3366CC>Marcus Aurelius</color>, who spent time on the Empire's

northern border fighting <color=#3366CC>Germanic</color>, Pictish and Scottish tribes. <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> was <color=#3366CC>legalised</color> by <color=#3366CC>Constantine I</color> in 313 CE
after three centuries of imperial persecution. Constantine also permanently moved the capital of the empire from Rome
to the city of <color=#3366CC>Byzantium</color> (modern-day <color=#3366CC>Istanbul</color>) which was renamed <color=#3366CC>Constantinople</color> in his honour in 330 CE. Christianity
became the sole official religion of the empire in 380 CE, and in 391–392 CE the emperor <color=#3366CC>Theodosius</color> outlawed pagan
religions. This is sometimes considered to mark the end of antiquity; alternatively antiquity is considered to end with the
<color=#3366CC>fall of the Western Roman Empire</color> in 476 CE; the closure of the pagan <color=#3366CC>Platonic Academy of Athens</color> in 529 CE; or the
rise of Islam in the early 7th century CE. During most of its existence, the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> was one of the most
powerful economic, cultural, and military forces in Europe.
Early Middle Ages
During the <color=#3366CC>decline of the Roman Empire</color>, Europe entered a long period of change arising from what historians call the
"<color=#3366CC>Age of Migrations</color>". There were numerous invasions and migrations amongst the <color=#3366CC>Ostrogoths</color>, <color=#3366CC>Visigoths</color>, <color=#3366CC>Goths</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Vandals</color>, <color=#3366CC>Huns</color>, <color=#3366CC>Franks</color>, <color=#3366CC>Angles</color>, <color=#3366CC>Saxons</color>, <color=#3366CC>Slavs</color>, <color=#3366CC>Avars</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bulgars</color>, <color=#3366CC>Vikings</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pechenegs</color>, <color=#3366CC>Cumans</color>, and Magyars.
<color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color> thinkers such as <color=#3366CC>Petrarch</color> would later refer to this as the "Dark Ages".
Isolated monastic communities were the only places to safeguard and compile written knowledge accumulated
previously; apart from this, very few written records survive. Much literature, philosophy, mathematics, and other
thinking from the classical period disappeared from Western Europe, though they were preserved in the east, in the
Byzantine Empire.
While the Roman empire in the west continued to decline, Roman traditions and the Roman state remained strong in
the predominantly Greek-speaking territories in the east, known as the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color>. During most of its existence,
the Byzantine Empire was the most powerful economic, cultural, and military force in Europe. Emperor <color=#3366CC>Justinian I</color>
presided over Constantinople's first golden age: he established a legal code that forms the basis of many modern legal
systems, funded the construction of the <color=#3366CC>Hagia Sophia</color> and brought the Christian church under state control.
From the 7th century onwards, as the Byzantines and neighbouring <color=#3366CC>Sasanid Persians</color> were severely weakened due to
the protracted, centuries-lasting and frequent <color=#3366CC>Byzantine–Sasanian wars</color>, the Muslim Arabs began to make inroads into
historically Roman territory, taking the Levant and North Africa and making inroads into <color=#3366CC>Asia Minor</color>. In the mid-7th
century, following the <color=#3366CC>Muslim conquest of Persia</color>, Islam penetrated into the <color=#3366CC>Caucasus</color> region. Over the next centuries
Muslim forces took Cyprus, <color=#3366CC>Malta</color>, Crete, <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>, and parts of southern Italy. Between 711 and 720, most of the lands of

the <color=#3366CC>Visigothic Kingdom</color> of <color=#3366CC>Iberia</color> were brought under <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color> rule—save for small areas in the northwest (<color=#3366CC>Asturias</color>) and
largely <color=#3366CC>Basque</color> regions in the <color=#3366CC>Pyrenees</color>. This territory, under the Arabic name <color=#3366CC>Al-Andalus</color>, became part of the
expanding <color=#3366CC>Umayyad Caliphate</color>. The unsuccessful <color=#3366CC>second siege of Constantinople</color> (717) weakened the <color=#3366CC>Umayyad</color>
<color=#3366CC>dynasty</color> and reduced their prestige. The Umayyads were then defeated by the <color=#3366CC>Frankish</color> leader <color=#3366CC>Charles Martel</color> at the
<color=#3366CC>Battle of Poitiers</color> in 732, which ended their northward advance. In the remote regions of north-western Iberia and the
middle Pyrenees the power of the Muslims in the south was scarcely felt. It was here that the foundations of the
Christian kingdoms of <color=#3366CC>Asturias</color>, <color=#3366CC>Leon</color>, and Galicia were laid and from where the reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula
would start. However, no coordinated attempt would be made to drive the <color=#3366CC>Moors</color> out. The Christian kingdoms were
mainly focused on their own internal power struggles. As a result, the <color=#3366CC>Reconquista</color> took the greater part of eight
hundred years, in which period a long list of Alfonsos, Sanchos, Ordoños, Ramiros, Fernandos, and Bermudos would
be fighting their Christian rivals as much as the Muslim invaders.
During the Dark Ages, the <color=#3366CC>Western Roman Empire</color> fell under the control of various tribes. The Germanic and Slav
tribes established their domains over Western and Eastern Europe, respectively. Eventually the Frankish tribes were
united under <color=#3366CC>Clovis I</color>. <color=#3366CC>Charlemagne</color>, a Frankish king of the <color=#3366CC>Carolingian</color> dynasty who had conquered most of Western
Europe, was anointed "Holy Roman Emperor" by the Pope in 800. This led to the founding of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>
in 962, which eventually became centred on the German principalities of central Europe.
East Central Europe saw the creation of the first Slavic states and the adoption of <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color> (c. 1000 CE). The
powerful <color=#3366CC>West Slavic</color> state of <color=#3366CC>Great Moravia</color> spread its territory all the way south to the Balkans, reaching its largest
territorial extent under <color=#3366CC>Svatopluk I</color> and causing a series of armed conflicts with <color=#3366CC>East Francia</color>. Further south, the first
<color=#3366CC>South Slavic states</color> emerged in the late 7th and 8th century and adopted Christianity: the <color=#3366CC>Bulgarian Empire</color>, the Serbian
Principality (later <color=#3366CC>Kingdom</color> and Empire), and the Duchy of Croatia (later <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Croatia</color>). To the east, <color=#3366CC>Kievan Rus'</color>
expanded from its capital in <color=#3366CC>Kiev</color> to become the largest state in Europe by the 10th century. In 988, <color=#3366CC>Vladimir the Great</color>
adopted <color=#3366CC>Orthodox Christianity</color> as the religion of state. Further east, <color=#3366CC>Volga Bulgaria</color> became an Islamic state in the 10th
century, but was eventually absorbed into Russia several centuries later.
High and Late Middle Ages
The period between the year 1000 and 1250 is known as the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color>, followed by the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color> until
During the High Middle Ages the population of Europe experienced significant growth, culminating in the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance</color>
<color=#3366CC>of the 12th century</color>. Economic growth, together with the lack of safety on the mainland trading routes, made possible
the development of major commercial routes along the coast of the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> and <color=#3366CC>Baltic Seas</color>. The growing wealth
and independence acquired by some coastal cities gave the <color=#3366CC>Maritime Republics</color> a leading role in the European scene.
The Middle Ages on the mainland were dominated by the two upper echelons of the social structure: the nobility and
the clergy. <color=#3366CC>Feudalism</color> developed in <color=#3366CC>France</color> in the Early Middle Ages, and soon spread throughout Europe. A struggle
for influence between the <color=#3366CC>nobility</color> and the <color=#3366CC>monarchy</color> in England led to the writing of <color=#3366CC>Magna Carta</color> and the establishment
of a <color=#3366CC>parliament</color>. The primary source of culture in this period came from the <color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic Church</color>. Through
monasteries and cathedral schools, the Church was responsible for education in much of Europe.
The <color=#3366CC>Papacy</color> reached the height of its power during the High Middle Ages. An <color=#3366CC>East-West Schism</color> in 1054 split the former
Roman Empire religiously, with the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Orthodox Church</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Byzantine Empire</color> and the Roman Catholic Church
in the former Western Roman Empire. In 1095 <color=#3366CC>Pope Urban II</color> called for a <color=#3366CC>crusade</color> against <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color> occupying

<color=#3366CC>Jerusalem</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Holy Land</color>. In Europe itself, the Church organised the <color=#3366CC>Inquisition</color> against heretics. In the <color=#3366CC>Iberian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Peninsula</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Reconquista</color> concluded with the fall of Granada in 1492, ending over seven centuries of Islamic rule in
the south-western peninsula.
In the east, a resurgent Byzantine Empire recaptured Crete and Cyprus from the Muslims, and reconquered the
Balkans. Constantinople was the largest and wealthiest city in Europe from the 9th to the 12th centuries, with a
population of approximately 400,000. The Empire was weakened following the defeat at <color=#3366CC>Manzikert</color>, and was weakened
considerably by the <color=#3366CC>sack of Constantinople in 1204</color>, during the <color=#3366CC>Fourth Crusade</color>. Although it would recover
Constantinople in 1261, <color=#3366CC>Byzantium</color> <color=#3366CC>fell in 1453</color> when <color=#3366CC>Constantinople was taken</color> by the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>.
In the 11th and 12th centuries, constant incursions by nomadic <color=#3366CC>Turkic</color> tribes, such as the <color=#3366CC>Pechenegs</color> and the
<color=#3366CC>Cuman-Kipchaks</color>, caused a massive migration of <color=#3366CC>Slavic</color> populations to the safer, heavily forested regions of the north,
and temporarily halted the expansion of Kievan Rus' to the south and east. The <color=#3366CC>Mongols invaded Europe</color> in the
mid-13th century, and together with their mostly Turkic subjects, became known as <color=#3366CC>Tatars</color>. These Tatars ruled the
Russian principalities through vassalage for the next 200 years. After the collapse of Mongol dominions, the first
Romanian states (principalities) emerged in the 14th century: <color=#3366CC>Moldavia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Walachia</color>. Previously, these territories were
under the successive control of Pechenegs and Cumans. The <color=#3366CC>Grand Principality of Moscow</color> became the dominant
Russian principality, forming in the process a centralized, autocratic Russian state by the late 15th century. The <color=#3366CC>Great</color>
<color=#3366CC>Stand on the Ugra River</color> in 1480 traditionally marks the end of the "Tatar yoke" over Russia.
The Great Famine of 1315–1317 was the first <color=#3366CC>crisis</color> that would strike Europe in the late Middle Ages. The period
between 1348 and 1420 witnessed the heaviest loss. The population of France was reduced by half. Medieval Britain
was afflicted by 95 famines, and France suffered the effects of 75 or more in the same period. Europe was devastated
in the mid-14th century by the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color>, one of the most deadly <color=#3366CC>pandemics</color> in human history which killed an
estimated 25 million people in Europe alone—a third of the European population at the time.
The plague had a devastating effect on Europe's social structure; it induced people to live for the moment as illustrated
by <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Boccaccio</color> in <color=#3366CC>The Decameron</color> (1353). It was a serious blow to the Roman Catholic Church and led to
increased persecution of Jews, beggars and <color=#3366CC>lepers</color>. The plague is thought to have returned every generation with
varying virulence and mortalities until the 18th century. During this period, more than 100 plague epidemics swept
across Europe.
Early modern period
The Renaissance was a period of cultural change originating in <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, and later spreading to the rest of Europe. The
rise of a new humanism was accompanied by the recovery of forgotten <color=#3366CC>classical Greek</color> and Arabic knowledge from
monastic libraries, often translated from Arabic into <color=#3366CC>Latin</color>. The Renaissance spread across Europe between the 14th
and 16th centuries: it saw the flowering of <color=#3366CC>art</color>, <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>music</color>, and the sciences, under the joint patronage of royalty,
the nobility, the <color=#3366CC>Catholic Church</color> and an emerging merchant class. Patrons in Italy, including the <color=#3366CC>Medici</color> family of
Florentine bankers and the <color=#3366CC>popes</color> in <color=#3366CC>Rome</color>, funded prolific quattrocento and cinquecento artists such as <color=#3366CC>Raphael</color>,
<color=#3366CC>Michelangelo</color> and <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color>.
Political intrigue within the Church in the mid-14th century caused the <color=#3366CC>Western Schism</color>. During this 40-year period, two
popes—one in <color=#3366CC>Avignon</color> and one in Rome—claimed rulership over the Church. Although the schism was eventually
healed in 1417, the papacy's spiritual authority had suffered greatly. In the 15th century, Europe started to extend itself
beyond its geographic frontiers. Spain and Portugal, the greatest naval powers of the time, took the lead in exploring
the world. Exploration reached the <color=#3366CC>Southern Hemisphere</color> in the Atlantic and the southern tip of Africa. <color=#3366CC>Christopher</color>
<color=#3366CC>Columbus</color> reached the <color=#3366CC>New World</color> in 1492, and <color=#3366CC>Vasco da Gama</color> opened the ocean route to the East, linking the
Atlantic and <color=#3366CC>Indian Oceans</color> in 1498. The Portuguese-born explorer <color=#3366CC>Ferdinand Magellan</color> reached Asia westward across
the Atlantic and the <color=#3366CC>Pacific Oceans</color> in a Spanish expedition, resulting in the first circumnavigation of the globe,
completed by the Spaniard <color=#3366CC>Juan Sebastián Elcano</color> (1519–1522). Soon after, the Spanish and Portuguese began
establishing large global empires in the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color>, Asia, Africa and Oceania. France, the <color=#3366CC>Netherlands</color> and England
soon followed in building large colonial empires with vast holdings in Africa, the Americas and Asia. In 1588, the
<color=#3366CC>Spanish Armada</color> failed to invade England. A year later, England tried unsuccessfully to invade Spain, allowing <color=#3366CC>Philip II</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Spain</color> to maintain his dominant war capacity in Europe. This English disaster also allowed the Spanish fleet to retain
its capability to wage war for the next decades. However, two more Spanish armadas failed to invade England (2nd
Spanish Armada and 3rd Spanish Armada).
The Church's power was further weakened by the <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>, which began in 1517 when German theologian <color=#3366CC>Martin</color>
<color=#3366CC>Luther</color> nailed his <color=#3366CC>Ninety-five Theses</color> criticising the selling of indulgences to the church door. He was subsequently
excommunicated in the papal bull Exsurge Domine in 1520 and his followers were condemned in the 1521 Diet of
Worms, which divided German princes between <color=#3366CC>Protestant</color> and Catholic faiths. <color=#3366CC>Religious fighting and warfare</color> spread
with Protestantism. The plunder of the empires of the Americas allowed Spain to finance <color=#3366CC>religious persecution</color> in
Europe for over a century. The <color=#3366CC>Thirty Years' War</color> (1618–1648) crippled the Holy Roman Empire and devastated much
of Germany, killing between 25 and 40 percent of its population. In the aftermath of the <color=#3366CC>Peace of Westphalia</color>, France
rose to predominance within Europe. The defeat of the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Turks</color> at the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Vienna</color> in 1683 marked the
historic end of <color=#3366CC>Ottoman expansion into Europe</color>.
In much of Central and Eastern Europe, the 17th century was a period of general decline; the region experienced more
than 150 famines in a 200-year period between 1501 and 1700. From the Union of Krewo (1385) east-central Europe
was dominated by the Kingdom of Poland and the <color=#3366CC>Grand Duchy of Lithuania</color>. The hegemony of the vast
<color=#3366CC>Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</color> had ended with the devastation brought by the <color=#3366CC>Northern War of 1655–1660</color> (Deluge)
and subsequent conflicts; the state itself was <color=#3366CC>partitioned</color> and ceased to exist at the end of the 18th century.
From the 15th to 18th centuries, when the disintegrating khanates of the <color=#3366CC>Golden Horde</color> were conquered by <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>,
Tatars from the <color=#3366CC>Crimean Khanate</color> frequently raided Eastern Europe to capture slaves. Further east, the Nogai Horde
and <color=#3366CC>Kazakh Khanate</color> frequently raided the Slavic-speaking areas of contemporary Russia and Ukraine for hundreds of
years, until the Russian expansion and conquest of most of northern Eurasia (i.e. Eastern Europe, Central Asia and
Siberia).
The Renaissance and the New Monarchs marked the start of an Age of Discovery, a period of exploration, invention
and scientific development. Important figures of the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color> during the 16th and 17th centuries included

<color=#3366CC>Copernicus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kepler</color>, <color=#3366CC>Galileo</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Isaac Newton</color>. According to Peter Barrett, "It is widely accepted that 'modern science'
arose in the Europe of the 17th century (towards the end of the Renaissance), introducing a new understanding of the
natural world."
18th and 19th centuries
The <color=#3366CC>Seven Years' War</color> brought to an end the "Old System" of alliances in Europe. Consequently, when the <color=#3366CC>American</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolutionary War</color> turned into a global war between 1778 and 1783, Britain found itself opposed by a strong coalition of
European powers, and lacking any substantial ally.
The Age of Enlightenment was a powerful intellectual movement during the 18th century promoting scientific and
reason-based thoughts. Discontent with the aristocracy and clergy's monopoly on political power in France resulted in
the French Revolution, and the establishment of the First Republic as a result of which the monarchy and many of the
nobility perished during the initial <color=#3366CC>reign of terror</color>. <color=#3366CC>Napoleon</color> Bonaparte rose to power in the aftermath of the French
Revolution, and established the <color=#3366CC>First French Empire</color> that, during the <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic Wars</color>, grew to encompass large parts
of Europe before collapsing in 1815 with the <color=#3366CC>Battle of Waterloo</color>. <color=#3366CC>Napoleonic rule</color> resulted in the further dissemination of
the ideals of the French Revolution, including that of the <color=#3366CC>nation state</color>, as well as the widespread adoption of the French
models of administration, <color=#3366CC>law</color> and education. The <color=#3366CC>Congress of Vienna</color>, convened after Napoleon's downfall, established

a new <color=#3366CC>balance of power</color> in Europe centred on the five "<color=#3366CC>great powers</color>": the UK, France, <color=#3366CC>Prussia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Austria</color>, and Russia.
This balance would remain in place until the <color=#3366CC>Revolutions of 1848</color>, during which liberal uprisings affected all of Europe
except for Russia and the UK. These revolutions were eventually put down by conservative elements and few reforms
resulted. The year 1859 saw the unification of Romania, as a nation state, from smaller principalities. In 1867, the
<color=#3366CC>Austro-Hungarian empire</color> was formed; 1871 saw the unifications of both <color=#3366CC>Italy</color> and <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> as nation-states from
smaller principalities.
In parallel, the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Question</color> grew more complex ever since the Ottoman defeat in the Russo-Turkish War
(1768–1774). As the dissolution of the Ottoman Empire seemed imminent, the <color=#3366CC>Great Powers</color> struggled to safeguard
their strategic and commercial interests in the Ottoman domains. The <color=#3366CC>Russian Empire</color> stood to benefit from the decline,
whereas the <color=#3366CC>Habsburg Empire</color> and Britain perceived the preservation of the Ottoman Empire to be in their best
interests. Meanwhile, the Serbian Revolution (1804) and <color=#3366CC>Greek War of Independence</color> (1821) marked the beginning of
the end of Ottoman rule in the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>, which ended with the <color=#3366CC>Balkan Wars</color> in 1912–1913. Formal recognition of the de
facto independent principalities of <color=#3366CC>Montenegro</color>, Serbia and <color=#3366CC>Romania</color> ensued at the <color=#3366CC>Congress of Berlin</color> in 1878, when
Bulgaria also gained de facto independence.
The <color=#3366CC>Industrial Revolution</color> began in <color=#3366CC>Great Britain</color> in the last part of the 18th century and spread throughout Europe. The
invention and implementation of new technologies resulted in rapid urban growth, mass employment and the rise of a
new working class. Reforms in social and economic spheres followed, including the first laws on <color=#3366CC>child labour</color>, the
legalisation of <color=#3366CC>trade unions</color>, and the abolition of slavery. In Britain, the Public Health Act 1875 was passed, which
significantly improved living conditions in many British cities. Europe's population increased from about 100 million in
1700 to 400 million by 1900. The last major famine recorded in Western Europe, the <color=#3366CC>Great Famine of Ireland</color>, caused
death and mass emigration of millions of Irish people. In the 19th century, 70 million people left Europe in migrations to
various European colonies abroad and to the United States. The industrial revolution also led to large population
growth, and the reached a peak of slightly above 25% around the year 1913.
20th century to the present
Two world wars and an economic depression dominated the first half of the 20th century. The First World War was
fought between 1914 and 1918. It started when <color=#3366CC>Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria</color> was assassinated by the
Yugoslav nationalist <color=#3366CC>Gavrilo Princip</color>. Most European nations were drawn into the war, which was fought between the

<color=#3366CC>Entente Powers</color> (France, the <color=#3366CC>United Kingdom</color>, <color=#3366CC>Russia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Belgium</color>, <color=#3366CC>Serbia</color>, and later <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>, <color=#3366CC>Greece</color>, <color=#3366CC>Romania</color>, Portugal, and

the United States) and the <color=#3366CC>Central Powers</color> (<color=#3366CC>Austria-Hungary</color>, <color=#3366CC>Germany</color>, <color=#3366CC>Bulgaria</color>, and the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>). The war
left more than 16 million civilians and military dead. Over 60 million European soldiers were mobilised from 1914 to
Russia was plunged into the <color=#3366CC>Russian Revolution</color>, which threw down the <color=#3366CC>Tsarist monarchy</color> and replaced it with the
<color=#3366CC>communist</color> <color=#3366CC>Soviet Union</color>, leading also to the independence of many former Russian governorates, such as <color=#3366CC>Finland</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Estonia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Latvia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Lithuania</color>, as new European countries. <color=#3366CC>Austria-Hungary</color> and the Ottoman Empire collapsed and
broke up into separate nations, and many other nations had their borders redrawn. The <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Versailles</color>, which
officially ended the First World War in 1919, was harsh towards Germany, upon whom it placed full responsibility for the
war and imposed heavy sanctions. Excess deaths in Russia over the course of the First World War and the <color=#3366CC>Russian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Civil War</color> (including the postwar <color=#3366CC>famine</color>) amounted to a combined total of 18 million. In 1932–1933, under <color=#3366CC>Stalin</color>'s
leadership, confiscations of grain by the Soviet authorities contributed to the <color=#3366CC>second Soviet famine</color> which caused
millions of deaths; surviving kulaks were persecuted and many sent to <color=#3366CC>Gulags</color> to do <color=#3366CC>forced labour</color>. Stalin was also
responsible for the <color=#3366CC>Great Purge</color> of 1937–38 in which the NKVD executed 681,692 people; millions of people were
<color=#3366CC>deported and exiled</color> to remote areas of the Soviet Union.
The social revolutions sweeping through Russia also affected other European nations following <color=#3366CC>The Great War</color>: in
1919, with the <color=#3366CC>Weimar Republic</color> in Germany and the First Austrian Republic; in 1922, with <color=#3366CC>Mussolini</color>'s one-party <color=#3366CC>fascist</color>
government in the Kingdom of Italy and in <color=#3366CC>Atatürk</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Turkish Republic</color>, adopting the Western alphabet and state
<color=#3366CC>secularism</color>. Economic instability, caused in part by debts incurred in the First World War and 'loans' to Germany played
havoc in Europe in the late 1920s and 1930s. This, and the <color=#3366CC>Wall Street crash of 1929</color>, brought about the worldwide
<color=#3366CC>Great Depression</color>. Helped by the economic crisis, social instability and the threat of communism, <color=#3366CC>fascist movements</color>
developed throughout Europe placing <color=#3366CC>Adolf Hitler</color> in power of what became <color=#3366CC>Nazi Germany</color>.
In 1933, Hitler became the leader of Germany and began to work towards his goal of building Greater Germany.
Germany re-expanded and took back the <color=#3366CC>Saarland</color> and Rhineland in 1935 and 1936. In 1938, <color=#3366CC>Austria</color> became a part of
Germany following the <color=#3366CC>Anschluss</color>. Following the <color=#3366CC>Munich Agreement</color> signed by Germany, France, the United Kingdom,
and Italy, later in 1938 Germany annexed the Sudetenland, which was a part of <color=#3366CC>Czechoslovakia</color> inhabited by ethnic
Germans. In early 1939, the remainder of Czechoslovakia was split into the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia,
controlled by Germany and the Slovak Republic. At the time, the United Kingdom and France preferred a policy of
<color=#3366CC>appeasement</color>.
With tensions mounting between Germany and Poland over the future of <color=#3366CC>Danzig</color>, the Germans turned to the Soviets
and signed the <color=#3366CC>Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact</color>, which allowed the Soviets to invade the Baltic states and parts of Poland and
Romania. Germany <color=#3366CC>invaded Poland</color> on 1 September 1939, prompting France and the United Kingdom to declare war
on Germany on 3 September, opening the European theatre of the Second World War. The <color=#3366CC>Soviet invasion of Poland</color>
started on 17 September and Poland fell soon thereafter. On 24 September, the Soviet Union attacked the Baltic
countries and, on 30 November, Finland, the latter of which was followed by the devastating <color=#3366CC>Winter War</color> for the Red
Army. The British hoped to land at Narvik and send troops to aid Finland, but their primary objective in the landing was
to encircle Germany and cut the Germans off from Scandinavian resources. Around the same time, Germany moved
troops into Denmark. The Phoney War continued.
In May 1940, Germany <color=#3366CC>attacked France</color> through the Low Countries. France capitulated in June 1940. By August,
Germany had begun a <color=#3366CC>bombing offensive against the United Kingdom</color> but failed to convince the Britons to give up. In
1941, Germany invaded the Soviet Union in <color=#3366CC>Operation Barbarossa</color>. On 7 December 1941 <color=#3366CC>Japan</color>'s <color=#3366CC>attack on Pearl</color>
<color=#3366CC>Harbor</color> drew the United States into the conflict as allies of the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color>, and other <color=#3366CC>allied</color> forces.
After the staggering <color=#3366CC>Battle of Stalingrad</color> in 1943, the German offensive in the Soviet Union turned into a continual
fallback. The <color=#3366CC>Battle of Kursk</color>, which involved the largest tank battle in history, was the last major German offensive on
the <color=#3366CC>Eastern Front</color>. In June 1944, British and American forces invaded France in the <color=#3366CC>D-Day landings</color>, opening a new
front against Germany. Berlin finally <color=#3366CC>fell in 1945</color>, ending the Second World War in Europe. The war was the largest and
most destructive in human history, with <color=#3366CC>60 million dead across the world</color>. More than 40 million people in Europe had
died as a result of the Second World War, including between 11 and 17 million people who perished during <color=#3366CC>the</color>
<color=#3366CC>Holocaust</color>. The Soviet Union lost around 27 million people (mostly civilians) during the war, about half of all Second
World War casualties. By the end of the Second World War, Europe had more than 40 million <color=#3366CC>refugees</color>. Several
post-war expulsions in Central and Eastern Europe displaced a total of about 20 million people.
The First World War, and especially the Second World War, diminished the eminence of Western Europe in world
affairs. After the Second World War the map of Europe was redrawn at the <color=#3366CC>Yalta Conference</color> and divided into two
blocs, the Western countries and the communist Eastern bloc, separated by what was later called by <color=#3366CC>Winston Churchill</color>
an "<color=#3366CC>Iron Curtain</color>". The United States and Western Europe established the <color=#3366CC>NATO</color> alliance and, later, the Soviet Union
and Central Europe established the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color>. Particular hot spots after the Second World War were <color=#3366CC>Berlin</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Trieste</color>, whereby the Free Territory of Trieste, founded in 1947 with the UN, was dissolved in 1954 and 1975,
respectively. The Berlin blockade in 1948 and 1949 and the construction of the <color=#3366CC>Berlin Wall</color> in 1961 were one of the
great international crises of the <color=#3366CC>Cold War</color>.
The two new <color=#3366CC>superpowers</color>, the United States and the Soviet Union, became locked in a fifty-year-long Cold War,
centred on <color=#3366CC>nuclear proliferation</color>. At the same time <color=#3366CC>decolonisation</color>, which had already started after the First World War,
gradually resulted in the independence of most of the European colonies in Asia and Africa.
In the 1980s the <color=#3366CC>reforms</color> of <color=#3366CC>Mikhail Gorbachev</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Solidarity</color> movement in Poland weakened the previously rigid
communist system. The opening of the <color=#3366CC>Iron Curtain</color> at the Pan-European Picnic then set in motion a peaceful chain
reaction, at the end of which the <color=#3366CC>Eastern bloc</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Warsaw Pact</color> and other <color=#3366CC>communist states collapsed</color>, and the Cold
War ended. Germany was reunited, after the symbolic <color=#3366CC>fall of the Berlin Wall</color> in 1989 and the maps of Central and
Eastern Europe were redrawn once more. This made old previously interrupted cultural and economic relationships

possible, and previously isolated cities such as <color=#3366CC>Berlin</color>, <color=#3366CC>Prague</color>, <color=#3366CC>Vienna</color>, <color=#3366CC>Budapest</color> and <color=#3366CC>Trieste</color> were now again in the
centre of Europe.
<color=#3366CC>European integration</color> also grew after the Second World War. In 1949 the <color=#3366CC>Council of Europe</color> was founded, following a
speech by Sir <color=#3366CC>Winston Churchill</color>, with the idea of unifying Europe to achieve common goals. It includes all European

states except for <color=#3366CC>Belarus</color>, Russia, and <color=#3366CC>Vatican City</color>. The <color=#3366CC>Treaty of Rome</color> in 1957 established the <color=#3366CC>European Economic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Community</color> between six Western European states with the goal of a unified economic policy and common market. The
1967 Merger Treaty created a single Commission and Council for the <color=#3366CC>European Economic Community</color>, the <color=#3366CC>European</color>
<color=#3366CC>Coal and Steel Community</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Euratom</color>, while the three communities remained legally distinct. The <color=#3366CC>Maastricht Treaty</color>,
which entered into force in 1993, established the <color=#3366CC>European Union</color> and renamed the European Economic Community as

the European Community. The EU established <color=#3366CC>a parliament</color>, <color=#3366CC>a court</color> and <color=#3366CC>a central bank</color>, and introduced the <color=#3366CC>euro</color> as a
unified currency. Between 2004 and 2013, more Central European countries began joining, expanding the EU to 28
European countries and once more making Europe a major economical and political centre of power. However, the
United Kingdom withdrew from the EU on 31 January 2020, as a result of a June 2016 referendum on EU membership.
The <color=#3366CC>Russo-Ukrainian War</color> steeply escalated after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, marking
the largest humanitarian and refugee crisis in Europe since the Second World War and the <color=#3366CC>Yugoslav Wars</color>.
Geography
Europe makes up the western fifth of the <color=#3366CC>Eurasian</color> landmass. It has a higher ratio of coast to landmass than any other
continent or subcontinent. Its maritime borders consist of the Arctic Ocean to the north, the Atlantic Ocean to the west
and the Mediterranean, Black and Caspian Seas to the south. Land relief in Europe shows great variation within
relatively small areas. The southern regions are more mountainous, while moving north the terrain descends from the
high <color=#3366CC>Alps</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pyrenees</color> and <color=#3366CC>Carpathians</color>, through hilly uplands, into broad, low northern plains, which are vast in the east.
This extended lowland is known as the <color=#3366CC>Great European Plain</color> and at its heart lies the North German Plain. An arc of
uplands also exists along the north-western seaboard, which begins in the western parts of the islands of Britain and
Ireland, and then continues along the mountainous, <color=#3366CC>fjord</color>-cut spine of Norway.
This description is simplified. Subregions such as the <color=#3366CC>Iberian Peninsula</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Italian Peninsula</color> contain their own
complex features, as does mainland Central Europe itself, where the relief contains many plateaus, river valleys and
basins that complicate the general trend. Sub-regions like <color=#3366CC>Iceland</color>, Britain and Ireland are special cases. The former is
a land unto itself in the northern ocean that is counted as part of Europe, while the latter are upland areas that were
once joined to the mainland until <color=#3366CC>rising sea levels</color> cut them off.
The largest European lakes are located in the north of the continent. The <color=#3366CC>Volga</color> and <color=#3366CC>Danube</color> are the two longest rivers
of Europe. Europe's largest <color=#3366CC>waterfall</color> (by flow rate) are the Rhine Falls on the <color=#3366CC>Rhine</color>.
Climate
Europe lies mainly in the <color=#3366CC>temperate</color> climate zone of the northern hemisphere, where the <color=#3366CC>prevailing wind direction is</color>
<color=#3366CC>from the west</color>. The climate is milder in comparison to other areas of the same latitude around the globe due to the
influence of the <color=#3366CC>Gulf Stream</color>, an ocean current which carries warm water from the <color=#3366CC>Gulf of Mexico</color> across the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ocean</color> to Europe. The Gulf Stream is nicknamed "Europe's central heating", because it makes Europe's climate
warmer and wetter than it would otherwise be. The Gulf Stream not only carries warm water to Europe's coast but also
warms up the prevailing westerly winds that blow across the continent from the Atlantic Ocean.
Therefore, the average temperature throughout the year of Aveiro is 16 C, while it is only 13 C in <color=#3366CC>New York City</color> which
is almost on the same latitude, bordering the same ocean. Berlin, Germany; Calgary, Canada; and Irkutsk, in far
south-eastern Russia, lie on around the same latitude; January temperatures in Berlin average around 8 C-change
higher than those in Calgary and they are almost 22 C-change higher than average temperatures in Irkutsk.
The large water masses of the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>, which equalise the temperatures on an annual and daily average,
are also of particular importance. The water of the Mediterranean extends from the <color=#3366CC>Sahara</color> to the Alpine arc in its
northernmost part of the <color=#3366CC>Adriatic Sea</color> near <color=#3366CC>Trieste</color>.
In general, Europe is not just colder towards the north compared to the south, but it also gets colder from the west
towards the east. The climate is more oceanic in the west and less so in the east. This can be illustrated by the
following table of average temperatures at locations roughly following the 64th, 60th, 55th, 50th, 45th and 40th
<color=#3366CC>latitudes</color>. None of them is located at high altitude; most of them are close to the sea.
The average temperatures for the coldest month, as well as the annual average temperatures, drop from the west to
the east. For instance, Edinburgh is warmer than Belgrade during the coldest month of the year, although Belgrade is
around 10° of latitude farther south.
